platforms.title: Thyroid Nodule Found? A Routine Scan Is Likely Behind It
platforms.meta_description: A thyroid nodule found by chance on a scan is usually benign. Here is what TSH, ultrasound and a fine needle biopsy each tell you, per ATA patient guidance.
platforms.body_html:
You went in for a CT scan of your neck after a car accident, or an ultrasound for something else entirely, and the report mentions a thyroid nodule. Nobody was looking for it, and now it is all you can think about. That is a very common way for these lumps to turn up. According to the American Thyroid Association (ATA), most thyroid nodules cause no symptoms and are often found incidentally on imaging done for unrelated reasons, or during a routine physical exam.

Why a Routine Scan Is So Often Behind the Discovery

Nodules are extremely common. According to the ATA, by age 60, about one-half of all people have a thyroid nodule that can be found by examination or imaging, and that over 90% of such nodules are benign. The more sensitive the imaging, the more of these small, harmless lumps it picks up.

This is also why the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends against screening for thyroid cancer in adults without symptoms (a grade D recommendation from 2017). Its evidence review points to overdiagnosis: screening raises the number of cancers found without changing the death rate, and it names South Korea, where population ultrasound screening was widespread, as the best ecological evidence. The same review summarises autopsy studies in which 11.5% of thyroid glands contained papillary thyroid cancer, most of them tiny, in people who had never been diagnosed. In other words, plenty of people carry thyroid changes that would never have harmed them.

None of that means your nodule should be ignored. It means the next steps are designed to separate the many harmless nodules from the few that need treatment, without rushing everyone into surgery.

If You Do One Thing Before Your Appointment

Get the full imaging report and bring it, along with a list of your medicines. Here is what usually follows, step by step.

A blood test for TSH. Your doctor will feel the thyroid and usually order thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and sometimes thyroxine (T4). The ATA notes that most nodules, including cancerous ones, are non-functioning, so the tests are typically normal. A normal result does not rule anything in or out; it mainly tells your doctor whether the gland is over- or underactive. A nuclear scan is now reserved mostly for the rare nodules that make too much hormone.

A dedicated thyroid ultrasound. This painless test shows whether the nodule is solid or fluid-filled, measures it precisely, and looks for features that are more common in cancer. Those features, together with size, decide whether a biopsy is worth doing at all.

A fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy, if needed. The ATA describes it as a simple office procedure under ultrasound guidance. The needle is smaller in diameter than those used in most blood draws, and several samples are usually taken, typically between two and six passes. You usually do not need to fast, but blood thinners often have to be paused, so tell the clinic in advance. The procedure itself usually lasts less than 30 minutes, and results take anywhere from a few days to two weeks.

So What Do the Biopsy Results Actually Mean?

According to the ATA patient guide on FNA, results fall into the six categories of the Bethesda System. Benign results account for up to 70% of biopsies, with a malignancy risk typically under 3%; these nodules are generally checked with a follow-up ultrasound within 18 months. According to the same ATA guide, malignant results make up 3-7% of specimens and almost always lead to surgery. In the ATA's figures, suspicious-for-malignancy results carry a 60-75% chance of cancer. Two "indeterminate" groups sit in between: atypia of undetermined significance (5-15% risk) and follicular neoplasm (15-30% risk), where repeat biopsy or molecular testing can help. A non-diagnostic sample simply means not enough cells were collected, and the biopsy is repeated.

Before you leave your appointment, run through this short checklist: Do you know your TSH result? Did the ultrasound report describe the nodule as solid, cystic or mixed, and give a size? Was a biopsy recommended, and if not, when is the next ultrasound? Has your doctor heard about any family history of thyroid cancer or radiation to your head and neck in childhood? The USPSTF lists both as factors that raise risk. And if you notice new hoarseness, or trouble swallowing or breathing, do not wait for the next scan date. This article is general information and does not replace advice from your own doctor.

Sources: American Thyroid Association, "Thyroid Nodules" and "Fine Needle Aspiration Biopsy of Thyroid Nodules" patient brochures; U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, "Thyroid Cancer: Screening" (May 9, 2017).
